title: Efficacy of central nervous system stimulant treatment for cocaine dependence: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled clinical trials

claims.statement: In the nine placebo-controlled randomized trials published up to 2006 and pooled in one review (640 patients with cocaine dependence, 344 given a stimulant medicine and 296 placebo, all with psychological treatment as well), stimulant medicines did not detectably reduce how many people dropped out (relative risk 0.97, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.10, with no difference for any single medicine) or the proportion of urine samples positive for a cocaine breakdown product in the trials that reported it (0.94, 0.84 to 1.05 across six trials; 0.84, 0.67 to 1.04 leaving out bupropion). Only an exploratory analysis, which filled in cocaine use for three further trials as the average of their starting and final values and used per-protocol rather than all-randomized data for two dexamphetamine trials, found fewer positive samples with dexamphetamine (0.73, 0.60 to 0.90) and with the medicines pooled (0.87, 0.77 to 0.99); that signal rests on filled-in outcomes, on two trials by one research group, and in part on one treatment arm in which 42 of 46 people dropped out, and the review's own authors call per-protocol bias unlikely without testing it. Modafinil's estimate in the main analysis was not significant (0.73, 0.50 to 1.04). More people stopped taking a stimulant than placebo because of unwanted effects (15 of 344, 4.4%, against 4 of 296, 1.3%; p = 0.03), the most common being sleeping problems, anxiety and jitteriness; the review's statement that no serious unwanted effect was reported has no counterpart in its results, which describe the information on unwanted effects as too limited for conclusions, and several trials did not say how they were assessed. The trials were small (30 to 149 patients, 42 to 182 days), nearly 9 in 10 participants were men, about half were also dependent on opioids and most smoked or injected cocaine, and the review calculates that 144 to 584 patients per arm would have been needed to detect a difference, more than any trial had; its own confidence was rated critically low, and the two headline figures printed in its abstract appear nowhere in its results. Craving could not be pooled. This is the evidence up to 2006 only: later reviews of these medicines, including modafinil and methylphenidate, have not been read. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Castells et al. (2007), random-effects relative risks, medicine against placebo. Dropout: all stimulants 0.97 (95% CI 0.85 to 1.10), I² 0%; without bupropion 0.97 (0.85 to 1.11); dexamphetamine 0.90 (0.71 to 1.12); methylphenidate 1.15 (0.77 to 1.73); modafinil 1.07 (0.55 to 2.09); mazindol 0.93 (0.59 to 1.47); bupropion 0.86 (0.41 to 1.79); 167 of 344 against 138 of 296 dropped out. Cocaine-positive urine, main analysis of six trials: all stimulants 0.94 (0.84 to 1.05); without bupropion 0.84 (0.67 to 1.04); modafinil 0.73 (0.50 to 1.04), p = 0.08; dexamphetamine 0.81 (0.56 to 1.16); methylphenidate 1.09 (0.72 to 1.64); mazindol 0.53 (0.11 to 2.54); bupropion 0.98 (0.86 to 1.12). Exploratory analysis of nine trials with filled-in values: dexamphetamine 0.73 (0.60 to 0.90), p = 0.003; all stimulants 0.87 (0.77 to 0.99); without bupropion 0.82 (0.71 to 0.94); leaving out the one arm in which 42 of 46 people dropped out, the dexamphetamine estimate becomes 0.79 (0.62 to 1.00) (study card's calculation). Post hoc, the three trials requiring both cocaine and opioid dependence: dropout 0.85 (0.56 to 1.30), cocaine use 0.86 (0.68 to 1.09). Dropout for unwanted effects 15 of 344 (4.4%) against 4 of 296 (1.3%), p = 0.03. Absolute risks for the efficacy outcomes are not reported.
